name: Fiddle-Leaf Fig
summary: A tropical fig tree commonly kept as a large indoor foliage plant. The listed indoor dimensions belong to a general species account, not a particular cultivar or guaranteed room-size endpoint.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ficus lyrata. NC State identifies the fiddle-shaped leaves and distinguishes houseplant size from the much larger tropical tree form. No cultivar is specified.

cultivation.short: Bright indirect light and careful watering
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends bright indirect light or partial shade, moist but well-drained soil, and protection from overwatering and strong afternoon sun. These are container-houseplant recommendations, not a hydroponic nutrient or watering protocol.

growth.short: Large lyre-shaped leaves on an upright woody plant
growth.guidance: NC State describes a tropical evergreen tree with broad lyre-shaped leaves; as a houseplant it gives a broad height range of 2–10 feet. The actual size depends on growing conditions and no compact cultivar is implied.

propagation.short: Stem cutting is the documented route
propagation.guidance: NC State lists stem cutting as a propagation strategy. Seed collection or germination instructions are not supplied by the selected source.

problems.short: Watch for leaf scorch, leaf drop, and common indoor pests
problems.guidance: NC State notes that excess direct sun can scorch leaves and watering extremes or temperature changes can contribute to leaf drop. Scale, aphids, mealybugs, thrips, and spider mites may occur; sap may irritate skin and the plant is toxic if ingested.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Container tree care does not establish long-term hydroponic suitability.

evidence.note: NC State lists a vase-shaped, spreading habit; indoor size varies.

height.reason: A broad 2–10 ft houseplant range is not treated as a single mature height.

spread.reason: No selected source establishes a typical indoor mature spread.

spacing.reason: No indoor system-spacing evidence is available.

light.reason: Bright indirect window placement is not mapped to a grow-light tier.

name: Wax Plant
summary: An epiphytic, vining houseplant known for thick leaves and fragrant flowers. Cultivars such as Compacta and Krimson Queen are not implied by this species-level identity.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Hoya carnosa and describes it as a climbing epiphyte or lithophyte. NC State lists multiple cultivated forms, but this record is the species without a named cultivar.

cultivation.short: Bright indirect light and a loose, fast-draining medium
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends bright indirect light, a loose fast-draining potting mix, and allowing the medium to dry between waterings. Too-wet or too-dry soil can contribute to leaf drop. These are epiphytic-container recommendations, not hydroponic specifications.

growth.short: Vining stems may be trained or allowed to trail
growth.guidance: NC State describes Hoya carnosa as an evergreen climbing vine and notes that Hoya stems can be trained on a support or grown in hanging baskets. No fixed mature dimensions are assigned to this species profile.

propagation.guidance: NC State lists stem cutting as the propagation strategy for wax plant. The selected source does not provide a seed-starting protocol.

problems.short: Avoid waterlogged mix and monitor common pests
problems.guidance: NC State notes leaf drop under overly wet or dry conditions and lists aphids, spider mites, and mealybugs as pests that may affect Hoya. No cultivar-specific flowering schedule is assigned.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Epiphytic potting guidance and cuttings do not establish long-term hydroponic crop suitability.

growthHabits.reason: The profile describes a climbing vine, but climbing is not a supported controlled-vocabulary habit value.

height.reason: No general indoor mature height is selected.

spread.reason: No general indoor spread is selected.

name: Inch Plant
summary: A fast-growing trailing houseplant with striped leaves and purple undersides. Common names overlap with unrelated plants, so the scientific identity is used to disambiguate this entry.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Tradescantia zebrina. NC State describes the striped inch plant and warns through its common-name listings that “zebra plant” is also used for unrelated species. No cultivar is specified.

cultivation.short: Filtered light and evenly managed moisture
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends filtered sun, regular watering while allowing the soil to dry between waterings, and reducing watering in winter. It notes that full sun can intensify leaf color but may wash color out in more southern locations; low light can reduce color and cause lower-leaf loss. This is not mapped to an indoor grow-light tier.

growth.short: Trailing stems can be trimmed to manage a hanging or spreading plant
growth.guidance: NC State describes trailing stems that root at nodes and recommends spring pruning to contain growth and encourage denser foliage. Cut healthy removed stems can be used for propagation.

propagation.short: Stem cuttings root at the nodes
propagation.guidance: NC State documents stem cuttings and notes that stems root at their nodes. It does not give a seed-starting protocol for the commonly grown houseplant form.

problems.short: Avoid soggy soil and overcrowded, wet foliage
problems.guidance: NC State notes that soggy soil can cause root or stem rot and that overcrowding or wet foliage can contribute to leaf-spot or fungal disease. Aphids, mealybugs, scale, whiteflies, and spider mites may occur.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Houseplant care and node-rooting cuttings do not establish long-term hydroponic performance.

evidence.note: NC State describes trailing stems and spread; the separate detailed profile carries the creeping habit terminology.

height.reason: The cited height and spread depend on container and growing context; no indoor mature endpoint is assigned.

name: Corn Plant
summary: A slow-growing tropical evergreen commonly used as an indoor foliage plant. Numerous striped and plain-green cultivars exist; none is assigned to this species-level entry.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Dracaena fragrans. NC State describes corn plant and lists cultivars with different leaf colors and forms; this profile does not infer a cultivar such as Janet Craig or Lemon Lime.

cultivation.short: Filtered light and moist but well-drained potting mix
cultivation.guidance: NC State recommends bright to moderate filtered light, moist soil during active growth with reduced winter watering, drainage holes, and warm conditions. Direct sun may burn foliage and insufficient light may narrow leaves. These are container-houseplant instructions, not a nutrient-solution formula.

growth.short: Woody cane-like stems carry strap-shaped leaves
growth.guidance: NC State describes a slow-growing evergreen shrub with upright woody stems and spirally arranged strap-like leaves. The source gives broad dimensions across plant forms; this profile does not select one as a universal indoor mature size.

propagation.guidance: NC State lists stem cutting as a propagation strategy for Dracaena fragrans. No seed-starting protocol is provided by the selected houseplant source.

problems.short: Brown tips may reflect dry air or water sensitivity
problems.guidance: NC State notes brown leaf tips with low humidity and sensitivity to fluoride or accumulated salts; it also lists thrips and mealybugs. These symptoms are not treated as a single definitive diagnosis.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Potted-houseplant guidance does not establish suitability for a recirculating hydroponic system.
